title: How Pollinators Help Plants Make Seeds
summary: Follow one grain of pollen from flower to flower, and see how bees, other animals and even the wind help plants make seeds.
notes: Source: Missouri Botanical Garden education resources, Plants and Their Pollinators.

steps.title: Meet the pollen grain
sentences: A flower's anthers make tiny grains of pollen. A flower may also have a sticky tip called a stigma that can catch pollen.
Pollination happens when pollen reaches a stigma. It can come from the same flower or from a different flower of the same kind.
If the pollen is compatible, it can help the plant make a seed after fertilisation.
points: Pollination is a step toward making seeds

steps.title: Why a bee visits
sentences: A bee may visit a flower to drink nectar or collect pollen for food.
While it feeds, loose grains of pollen stick to its body. Some can rub off onto the stigma of the next flower it visits.
The bee gets food, and the plant gets help moving pollen.
points: Pollen sticks and moves with the bee
Some pollen rubs off on another flower

steps.title: Different flowers, different carriers
sentences: Bees are only one kind of pollinator. Some butterflies, moths, birds and bats also carry pollen.
Some plants, such as grasses, release pollen into the wind instead. Their flowers may have few obvious petals.
A tube-shaped flower can hold nectar where a long tongue or beak can reach it. The visitor may brush against pollen on the way in.
points: Animals and wind can move pollen
A flower's shape can affect which visitor reaches its nectar

steps.title: Try it with a cotton swab
sentences: Draw an anther on one piece of paper and a stigma on another. Colour the anther with a washable marker.
While the mark is wet, touch it with a cotton swab and then touch the second paper. The ink models pollen being carried between flowers.
Moving pollen happens before the seed forms. If wind or an animal moves the seed later, that is seed dispersal.
points: A cotton swab models a pollen carrier

facts: Some flowers open at night and can be visited by moths or bats.
Wind can carry grass pollen even when no animal visits the flowers.

quiz.q: A bee leaves a grain of pollen on a flower's stigma. What has just happened?
quiz.why: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to a stigma.

quiz.q: How can grass flowers receive pollen even when insects are absent?
options: They catch pollen carried by wind
quiz.why: Many grasses use wind to carry their pollen.

quiz.q: A bird eats a ripe berry and drops its seed elsewhere. Which process is that?
quiz.why: The seed has already formed. Moving it to a new place is dispersal.
